newsitem.title: ITALY: Minister denies Italian spies bugged Berlusconi.
newsitem.headline: Minister denies Italian spies bugged Berlusconi.

text.p: The Italian government said on Wednesday it had no evidence that intelligence agents bugged the office of opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi.
Addressing parliament on an issue that has whipped up a storm in Italy, Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano said any suggestion that the state might be involved was "arbitrary and irresponsible".

"Neither the government nor public opinion has any evidence that could lead one to think that organs of the state were engaged in unjustified eavesdropping on a member of parliament," he told the Chamber of Deputies (lower house).

Berlusconi, prime minister for seven months in 1994 and now leader of the centre-right opposition Freedom Alliance, called a news conference last Friday to show journalists a bugging device he said had been found at his Rome office.

The media mogul, who is on trial in Milan on corruption charges which he has portrayed as part of a political plot against him, has filed a formal complaint with magistrates following the discovery of the matchbox-sized device.
He has not said who he thinks may have planted the bug. Some of his allies have cast suspicion on what they refer to as "deviant offshoots" of Italy's intelligence services.

Police have also seized a floppy disk sent anonymously to an Italian news agency by a man claiming that he had made the device at the request of an unnamed member of parliament for the Lazio region, which includes the capital Rome.
Napolitano said the centre-left government would cooperate fully with magistrates' investigations into the Berlusconi bug.
He said the affair should be resolved rapidly in order to help calm the political climate.
Allegations of murky dealings and political plotting by some intelligence agents have surfaced regularly in Italian affairs for more than two decades.
More recently, the focus has switched to whether privacy is being invaded by magistrates who have investigated the graft scandals that have convulsed Italian life for four years.

The past month has seen widespread publication of transcripts of telephone taps conducted by magistrates in the northwest port of La Spezia leading inquiries into an alleged "super lobby" of corrupt businessmen, lawyers and judges.
